explainBack.prompt: Why does drawing a rough sketch or placing a comment on an image work better than writing a longer, more detailed prompt?
explainBack.response: Because a sketch carries spatial information directly — relative positions, sizes and empty space — that prose describes ambiguously, and a comment pins the edit to one region so the system regenerates only what you targeted while keeping the rest. A longer prompt forces every constraint through words, where the model must reconstruct your layout from description; the visual input hands it the layout ready-made. Crucially, the system still generates a new image each time, so precise text, measurements and brand details must be verified outside the picture.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: P005 (visual communication versus one long prompt), P006 (sketch as rough map, comment as smaller editing target, new-image limit), P010 (better context routes beat longer prompts).
explainBack.assessment: The article's mechanism fully supports this causal answer in ordinary language; the limit on editability survives the explanation, so explain-back passes.

unseenTransfer.prompt: Using this article's mechanism, how should she guide the tool, and what should she never trust the generated image to get right?
unseenTransfer.response: She should sketch the flyer's three zones — crest box top-left, map box bottom-right, centre column — so the spatial layout arrives as visual context rather than ambiguous prose, then add only the few must-keep details in words. If one region is wrong, she should place a comment on that region for a targeted regeneration instead of rewriting the whole prompt. Because the output is a generated image, not a design file with live text, she must verify the event times, translations and crest fidelity outside the picture — ideally having a designer rebuild final text — since factual copy inside a generated image is exactly what the article warns still needs external checking.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: The reasoning applies P006 (map/target mechanism and new-image limit), P007 (copy and factual details checked outside the picture) and P010 (prefer a better context route over a longer prompt) to a situation absent from the article.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The mechanism transfers cleanly and completely to this new scenario, including its limits, so transfer passes.

incidentExplained.observation: What was released, when, by whom, what it adds and what it does not change are all laid out causally.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: OpenAI released ChatGPT Images 2.5 on September 8. It is the image-making and image-editing part of ChatGPT—not a new general chat model. The release adds ways to begin with a rough drawing or a template, place a comment on part of an image you want changed, and share the prompt behind an image.

OpenAI says Images 2.5 is rolling out across all ChatGPT tiers on desktop, mobile and web, as well as ChatGPT Work and Codex. The release notes add two important limits: templates are not yet available in Work mode, and existing image-generation limits have not changed. Because this is a rollout, a feature may not appear in every account at the same moment.

OpenAI also says the underlying model keeps people and objects more consistent through several edits and can reduce the time it takes to generate an image by up to 50% compared with Images 2.0. Those performance figures are company claims. Axios tested early access and found better likeness preservation and more detailed editing in its own small set of tasks; that is useful first-hand evidence, not a broad independent benchmark.

termsExplainedInContext.observation: Sketch, comment-based editing and rollout are each given plain meaning at first meaningful use; 'context' is explained by example.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: OpenAI says Images 2.5 is rolling out across all ChatGPT tiers on desktop, mobile and web, as well as ChatGPT Work and Codex. The release notes add two important limits: templates are not yet available in Work mode, and existing image-generation limits have not changed. Because this is a rollout, a feature may not appear in every account at the same moment.

A sketch gives the system a rough map: put the sofa here, leave space for a headline there, or make the product the largest object. A comment gives it a smaller editing target: change this sleeve, remove that lamp, keep the rest. The AI still generates a new image; it is not turning the result into a fully editable design file with independent text boxes and layers.

The larger lesson is current AI practice: when the product gives you a better way to provide context—a picture, a file, a marked region or a shared project—use that route instead of forcing the whole job into a longer prompt.

readerConsequenceSpecific.observation: Consequences land in specific reader situations: a marketing manager's social post, a room plan, one's own plan limits.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: That distinction matters for real work. A marketing manager could sketch the arrangement of a social post, then ask for visual directions before a designer builds the final asset. Someone planning a room could draw the furniture placement instead of writing a paragraph about left, right and centre. But exact copy, measurements, brand rules and important factual details still need checking outside the finished picture.

If the new tools appear in your account, try them on a task where layout matters. Draw the rough arrangement first, add the few details that must be preserved, and make one targeted edit at a time. That tests the real improvement: whether you can steer the image without rebuilding the whole idea after every change.

Do not treat “all tiers” as unlimited use, or OpenAI's speed claim as a promise about every device and every image. Your plan's existing generation limits still apply, rollout timing can vary, and a complex request may still need several attempts.
